newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain's empire after Hong Kong-the last colonies.
newsitem.headline: Britain's empire after Hong Kong-the last colonies.

text.p: Hong Kong, Britain's richest and most populous remaining colony, reverts to Chinese rule on July 1. Here is a list of London's last colonial outposts, the remnants of a global empire on which it was once said the sun never set.

ANGUILLA -- A small, storm-battered island in the eastern Caribbean, colonised in 1650. It reverted to being a British territory after a period in the 1960s as an unwilling member of the Associated State of St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla.

BERMUDA -- Britain's oldest colony -- and after the return of Hong Kong its most populous -- was settled after a ship full of settlers heading for America foundered on its reefs in 1609. The economy was badly hit by the closure of a U.S. military base in 1995, but most voters among the more than 60,000 islanders voted against independence in a referendum that year.

BRITISH INDIAN OCEAN TERRITORY -- Ceded to Britain in 1814 and also claimed by Mauritius. The population was evicted after a U.S.-British pact that created the Diego Garcia military base, which was later used during the 1991 Gulf War.

BRITISH VIRGIN ISLANDS -- Discovered in 1493 by Christopher Columbus, this former Caribbean pirate haven was annexed in 1672 and settled by European planters and African slaves. Tourism and offshore financial services are now mainstays of the economy.

CAYMAN ISLANDS -- Low-lying coral islands that were settled in the 17th century and are now on the strategic route between illegal drug producers in South America and their North American markets. The wealthiest economy per capita in the Caribbean.

FALKLAND ISLANDS -- A wind-swept archipelago in the South Atlantic that has been contested at different times by France, Britain, Spain and Argentina. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, but was expelled by a British task force after fighting in which around 1,000 people were killed. Most of the 2,500 island residents oppose claims by Buenos Aires, which calls the group Las Malvinas. Britain maintains a powerful and expensive military presence on the potentially resource-rich islands.

GIBRALTAR -- A strategic port at the mouth of the Mediterranean that Britain seized from Spain in 1704 and later held through repeated sieges. Spain contests sovereignty and cut border links in the 1960s. But residents voted to stay British. In recent years London has rejected proposals to implement self-determination with British sovereignty because they lacked Spanish approval.

MONTSERRAT -- A Caribbean island settled in the 17th century. Plans to declare independence have been stalled by a series of destructive hurricanes and by the threat of a volcanic eruption that could make two-thirds of the island uninhabitable.

PITCAIRN ISLANDS -- A tiny volcanic island in the South Pacific settled in 1790 by mutineers from the HMS Bounty. The main government revenue for the island, which in 1995 had a population of 58, comes from the sale of postage stamps.

ST. HELENA -- A remote island in the South Atlantic most famous as Napoleon's place of exile after his defeat in the battle of Waterloo. Anger among some of the 5,500 residents over high unemployment and London's refusal to allow islanders to work in Britain has made headlines.
St. Helena has two dependent islands: ASCENSION, an important staging post in the 1982 Falklands war, and TRISTAN DA CUNHA, a volcanic outcrop that is home to around 300 people.

SOUTH GEORGIA and the SOUTH SANDWICH ISLANDS -- South Georgia, an icy island southeast of the Falkland Islands, was claimed by explorer Captain Cook in 1775. A small military detachment and research station are maintained on the island, which was briefly occupied by Argentina in 1982. The South Sandwich Islands are uninhabited.

TURKS AND CAICOS ISLANDS -- Caribbean islands settled by planters loyal to Britain after the American War of Independence (1771-1781), along with their slaves. Recent politics have been dominated by scandals over official involvement in illegal drug trafficking.

Britain also maintains two survey bases at the BRITISH ANTARCTIC TERRITORY which are open year-round with a population ranging from 50 to 150. Ownership of part of the territory is contested by Argentina and Chile. The area may include oil and gas reserves, but development is forbidden by international treaty.
